speaker: Jeff Currie
title: Jeff Currie on the 'Volatility Trap' Keeping Commodity Prices So High
question: In macro commodity markets, why can rising oil prices fail to drag down global growth the way they did in the 1970s and 2000s?
guest: If you just took a closed economy like the US and raised oil prices, all it is is a transfer from Chicago to Houston. If everybody had the same consumption and savings, it would have no impact. The reason the '70s and the 2000s had such an impact was the savings glut: you had a transfer from groups in the US consuming around 92% to groups consuming around 50 to 60%. As oil prices went up, dollars went to Saudi Arabia, and they took those excess dollars and bought US Treasuries. Why did they have to do that? They didn't have anything else to do with those dollars—the only market with enough liquidity to absorb that kind of investment was US Treasuries. Today, you can place $100 billion into China or Saudi Arabia immediately. Look at an entity like PIF in Saudi Arabia or similar entities in Abu Dhabi: their intention is to invest in power, gas, logistics, transportation, and healthcare in their own economy. So if the savings glut created a slowdown in growth from higher oil prices, a spending spree does the opposite—reducing the supply of dollars recycled back into the US, running up US funding costs, and creating more commodity inflation.

points.core: Higher commodity prices merely transfer income unless recipients spend less than payers.
points.note: Accept: in a closed system with equal marginal propensity to consume, higher oil prices are a neutral transfer rather than a growth drag. Do not credit: generic claims that inflation always hurts consumers.

points.note: Accept: earlier cycles shifted dollars from high-consumption Western economies to exporters with lower consumption rates, creating a savings glut. Do not credit: vague references to OPEC monopolies.

points.core: Exporters previously recycled surplus petrodollars into US Treasuries because local markets lacked depth.
points.note: Accept: oil exporters bought US government bonds because only Treasuries had enough liquidity to absorb massive inflows. Do not credit: generic claims about dollar reserve status.

points.core: Modern commodity exporters absorb windfalls domestically through sovereign funds instead of recycling dollars.
points.note: Accept: countries like Saudi Arabia or China now have domestic capacity and sovereign vehicles to spend windfalls locally, tightening dollar supply and boosting demand. Do not credit: generic claims about de-dollarization.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Rising oil prices hurt growth less today mainly because the world economy is far less oil-intensive and because the source of the price rise matters.

Oil used per unit of global GDP has fallen by more than half since the 1970s, thanks to efficiency gains, fuel switching and the shift toward services. A given price increase therefore takes a smaller bite out of household and business budgets.

The cause of the increase also matters. The 1970s shocks were supply disruptions, which act like a tax on consumers. Many later rallies, including much of the 2000s run-up, were driven by strong demand, so high prices were a symptom of growth, not a brake on it.

Other buffers have grown too. Central banks have more credible inflation targets, so oil spikes are less likely to feed wage-price spirals and force recession-inducing rate hikes. Wages are less indexed to inflation.

Finally, the US shale boom turned the largest consumer into a major producer. Higher prices now boost investment and income there, offsetting consumer pain, while exporters recycle their windfalls into global demand.

points.why: The response notes that producer gains offset consumer losses but never explains that the net growth effect depends on how much each group spends.
The response discusses what drove past oil rallies without identifying the transfer from high-spending importers to lower-spending exporters that created a savings glut.
The response omits both past petrodollar purchases of US Treasuries and the lack of comparably liquid investment markets.
The reference to global demand leaves unspecified how sovereign funds invest oil windfalls domestically and reduce dollar recycling into the US.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Rising oil prices weigh far less on global growth today because structural shifts have blunted the traditional oil tax. Global oil intensity per unit of GDP has more than halved since the 1970s and fallen further since the 2000s as economies shifted toward services, efficiency gains, and clean energy, shrinking fuel’s share of household and business budgets. Equally important, the shale revolution turned the United States from the heavy net importer of the 1970s and 2000s into a major net exporter: consumer losses at the pump are now largely offset by domestic energy revenues and capital investment, while short-cycle shale supply responds much faster than conventional fields to cap prolonged spikes. The shock’s origin also matters, since price gains driven by buoyant global demand rather than abrupt supply cutoffs reflect underlying economic strength. Finally, firmer inflation expectations and minimal automatic wage indexation prevent 1970s-style wage-price spirals, giving central banks more room to look through temporary energy shocks without triggering recessionary rate hikes.

points.why: The response describes domestic revenues and investment offsetting consumer losses but does not tie the growth effect of the transfer to how much recipients spend relative to payers.
The response notes past U.S. import dependence but does not explain how oil booms shifted income from high-spending importers to lower-spending exporters.
The response does not mention exporters buying U.S. Treasuries or explain why market depth drove those purchases.
The response discusses U.S. shale investment but does not explain how sovereign funds invest oil windfalls domestically and reduce dollar recycling.

noweb.answer: Rising oil prices inflict far less damage on global growth today because the world economy’s structural relationship with crude has fundamentally changed since the 1970s and 2000s. Global oil intensity—the volume of oil needed to generate a unit of GDP—has declined steadily due to efficiency gains, alternative energy adoption, and the shift from heavy industry toward services and digital output. Equally important, the post-2008 shale revolution transformed the United States from the world’s largest net oil importer into a net exporter; higher crude prices no longer act purely as a wealth transfer abroad, since consumer headwinds in the world's largest economy are partially offset by domestic energy investment and producer income, while flexible short-cycle shale supply dampens prolonged price spikes. Monetary transmission has also softened: weaker automatic wage indexation and better-anchored inflation expectations limit 1970s-style wage-price spirals, reducing pressure on central banks to hike economies into recession over temporary energy shocks. Finally, when oil rallies reflect resilient global aggregate demand rather than abrupt physical supply embargoes, underlying economic momentum helps absorb the higher costs.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Rising oil prices hurt growth less now mainly because economies use less oil and oil shocks travel through them differently. Global oil intensity, meaning barrels needed per dollar of GDP, has fallen by roughly half or more since the 1970s. Efficiency gains, the shift toward services, and fuel switching mean the same price jump takes a much smaller share of household and business income.

The cause of the rise also matters. The 1970s spikes were supply shocks from embargoes and revolutions. When prices rise because global demand is strong, as in much of the mid-2000s, they reflect growth rather than choke it off.

The shale revolution made the United States a net petroleum exporter. A higher price now moves income within the US economy, boosting energy investment, jobs and producer revenues instead of just sending money abroad. Exporters also tend to spend or recycle their windfalls more quickly than they did in the 1970s.

Finally, monetary policy has changed. Credible central banks with anchored inflation expectations and less wage indexation avoid the 1970s wage-price spiral, so they don't need recession-inducing rate hikes. A sharp, sustained supply shock, like the one in 2022, can still do real damage.

points.why: The response identifies a domestic income transfer but does not tie its growth effect to whether recipients spend as much as payers would have.
The response mentions money going abroad and slower windfall spending in the 1970s but does not identify the shift from high-spending importers to lower-spending exporters.
The response mentions recycling in general but never identifies US Treasuries or explains why their liquidity drew exporters’ surplus dollars.
The response claims faster spending or recycling but does not identify domestic sovereign-fund investment as the alternative to recycling dollars abroad.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Rising oil prices no longer weigh on global growth as heavily as they did in the 1970s and 2000s for several structural and cyclical reasons. First, the global economy is far less oil-intensive: decades of efficiency gains, a shift toward services and technology, and growing adoption of natural gas, renewables, and electric vehicles mean energy costs represent a much smaller share of GDP and household spending. Second, the geography of production has shifted. Because the United States is now a major net exporter rather than a large importer, higher crude prices stimulate domestic energy investment and incomes, offsetting much of the drag on consumers. Third, the source of the price rise matters—when oil climbs alongside strong global demand rather than a sudden supply shock, growth naturally stays resilient. Finally, modern central banks benefit from better-anchored inflation expectations and weaker wage-price indexation than in the 1970s, allowing policymakers to look through temporary energy spikes instead of hiking interest rates aggressively into a recession.

points.why: The response describes gains to domestic producers offsetting consumer losses but omits how the spending propensities of payers and recipients determine the net effect on growth.
The response mentions past US import dependence without explaining how earlier oil booms shifted income from high-spending importers to lower-spending exporters.
The response does not explain that exporters recycled surplus petrodollars into US Treasuries because local markets lacked the depth to absorb them.
The response discusses US energy investment but does not explain how modern exporters use sovereign funds to invest windfalls domestically and reduce dollar recycling.

Rising oil prices can slow global growth, but the effect depends on why prices rise and how much oil economies use. When strong demand pushes oil prices up, the increase can accompany an expansion. A supply disruption is more damaging because it raises fuel costs while reducing the amount of oil available.

The world also uses less oil per dollar of output than it did in the 1970s, thanks to more efficient vehicles and a shift toward services. Higher prices still squeeze consumers and oil importers, but they raise income for producers. The U.S. produces far more oil than it did in the 2000s, so some of the hit to U.S. household spending can be offset by gains in domestic production and investment. And when inflation expectations stay anchored, central banks have less reason to respond to a temporary fuel-price spike with sharp rate hikes. A large, sustained supply shock can still drag down growth.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
It matters why oil is rising. When strong global demand lifts the price, oil and GDP can rise together. Higher fuel costs still squeeze consumers, but the expansion that raised demand can outweigh that drag. A supply disruption, as in the 1970s, is more damaging because households and firms must pay more even as less oil is available.

The economy has also changed. Producing a dollar of global output takes less oil, so the same percentage price increase delivers a smaller hit. And higher prices redistribute income from importers to producers, some of whom spend or invest the proceeds. Since the 2000s, the rise of US shale has meant that some of the hit to American consumers is offset by domestic producers’ income and investment.

A large, sustained supply shock can still slow growth, especially if it feeds broader inflation and prompts central banks to raise interest rates.
